newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dlr draws breath after intervention comment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dlr draws breath after intervention comment.

text.p: A bruised dollar was trying to find its feet in Europe on Thursday after being hit by Japanese authorities' comments that Tokyo will step into the currency market when appropriate.

But analysts and traders said the dollar had just drawn breath after this week's breakneck rally to a 47-month high against the yen and a 31-month high on the mark, and also ahead of key economic events next month.
"The dollar came off quite a bit in Tokyo. Certainly Europe seemed unhappy with that level...and it's been nudging higher," said Pat Magill, head of corporate trading at Daiwa Europe.
At Europe's midday, the dollar was at 1.6303 marks and 121.70 yen, down from its late Wednesday European level of 1.6417 and 121.92 yen.

While the comment by Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, spooked dollar bulls, the market had then realised that it only reiterated Japan's view that too much currency volatility was undesireable.

"No-one seems to be displeased at the level (the dollar's) at, the comments seem to be directed at the speed at which it's been moving rather than anything else," said HSBC James Capel economist David Bloom.
But analysts said the comment by Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" in the currency market, carried more weight when combined with that of Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer.
On Wednesday Tietmeyer said he expected the "normalisation" of the mark against the dollar to end soon and that the mark will remain a strong currency.

"I think we're getting to the stage where not just Japan but the U.S. and Germany are saying that this far is fine but any further would probably be problematic," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.

Breedon said that even U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's remark overnight that the U.S. policy on the dollar has not changed could be interpreted as a watering down of his recent comments that a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest.
The dollar drew comfort from Rubin's comment overnight and analysts said its underlying sentiment was still firm.

Thursday's moves meant the market was lying low ahead Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to a Senate panel later on Thursday. It was also looking ahead to a meeting of the Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee next week and a meeting of the Group of Seven finance ministers and central bank governors in Berlin early next month.
"There's the G7 meeting coming up, and I think people are scared of trying to push the dollar too far and making a nasty communique come out against it," HSBC James Capel's Bloom said.

The market's conviction that the U.S. economy was in good health and that interest rates there would go up soon would sustain the dollar, although it was unlikely to rally at the dizzying speed seen before, analysts said.
"It's going to be a long time before people stop focusing on U.S. growth prospects," Lehman's Breedon said.
"If the U.S. doesn't raise rates at the next FOMC, I think the bull run will pause for breath. But that only means the market will worry about a hike in rates at the next FOMC," HSBC's Bloom said.
